Test it without special equipment

What would a vertical stick show?

A level surface, a known stick height and a measured shadow turn solar altitude into a direct observation.

Measured altitude formula altitude = arctan(stick ÷ shadow)

Keep the stick vertical and measure on level ground. Buildings, hills and atmospheric refraction matter close to the horizon.

Globe predictionNo direct Sun
Flat prediction2.2 m shadow

What perspective really predicts

Lower in the view, smaller in apparent size—but still above the plane

For an elevated local Sun, perspective is already contained in the line-of-sight triangle. As horizontal distance grows, its viewing angle approaches 0° but does not become negative. Its stated height above the plane never changes; only its apparent direction and size do.

flat altitude = arctan(height ÷ horizontal distance)

For anyone who wants to inspect the assumptions

Show the model and calculations

Exactly what is being compared?

Globe model: a distant Sun, a spherical Earth and the standard relationship between latitude, solar declination and hour angle.

Flat model: a north-pole-centred azimuthal-equidistant plane. The Sun circles the north pole once per solar day at a fixed height. Its ground-track radius follows the real solar declination so it can mimic the seasons as generously as possible.

Important: “Flat Earth” has no single agreed mathematical model. These results apply to this explicit model; changing it means stating and testing new assumptions.

Globe calculation

Solar hour angleH = 15° × (local solar time − 12)

Solar altitudesin a = sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ cos H

Shadow lengthL = stick height ÷ tan a

Here φ is latitude and δ is the Sun’s declination for the selected date. Sunrise and sunset use the conventional −0.833° centre altitude, which allows for the Sun’s radius and average horizon refraction.

Flat-plane calculation

Observer radius from north polerₒ = R × (90° − φ)

Sun-track radiusrₛ = R × (90° − δ)

Horizontal distanced = √(rₒ² + rₛ² − 2rₒrₛ cos θ)

Viewing altitudea = arctan(height ÷ d)

The plane uses R = 6,371 km only as a map scale. The viewing formula itself is ordinary Euclidean geometry.

Clock time and the Equation of Time

A clock is not a sundial. Longitude, time-zone offset and the Equation of Time shift clock noon away from apparent solar noon. In “clock time” mode this app converts the selected clock reading before calculating either model.

Equation of Time on this date−7.4 minutes

The Equation of Time varies because Earth’s axis is tilted and its orbit is slightly elliptical. It changes when the Sun reaches the meridian; it does not rescue a local elevated Sun from the geometric sunset problem.

Accuracy and limits

This is an educational comparison, not a survey instrument. The solar-coordinate method is the U.S. Naval Observatory’s approximately one-arcminute algorithm for dates within two centuries of 2000. Terrain, observer height, weather and changing refraction can still move an observed horizon crossing.

The strongest comparisons are made well away from a blocked horizon, or by measuring a noon shadow over several dates.
